Office styling and layout

knittogether reads Word documents through Pandoc, and Pandoc only understands a document’s structure. It can tell a heading from a paragraph, but not that someone made a line bold and 16 point. The more a Word document relies on styles rather than hand formatting, the better it converts. This article covers setting up Word documents and templates so that formatting survives the trip from Word to Markdown and back. For slides, see vignette("powerpoint").

Use Word’s built-in styles

Use Word’s own styles for everything: Title, Heading 1 to 6, Normal, List Paragraph and Caption. Pandoc turns them into Markdown like this:

Word style Markdown
Heading 1 #
Heading 2 ##
Heading 3 ###
Normal A plain paragraph
List Paragraph A - or 1. list
Caption A figure or table caption

If you want headings to look different, change the style (Home → Styles → right-click → Modify) rather than formatting each heading by hand. Hand formatting is lost on conversion. A changed style is kept, and you can carry it over to the output with a reference document (see below).

Some things don’t convert at all. Text boxes, SmartArt, WordArt and shapes with text in them are dropped or flattened. Turn them into ordinary text, or save them as an image with a caption.

In tables, avoid merged cells. Tables with long text or line breaks in cells may need different Pandoc settings, as described in vignette("extended-workflow").

Add captions with Insert Caption

Add captions to images and tables with Word’s own tool: right-click the image or table and choose Insert Caption. Pandoc then knows the caption belongs to the image or table. A caption typed underneath as ordinary text is just another paragraph.

Reference documents

A reference document is a Word file whose styles Quarto copies into the output. Point to it in the YAML of your .qmd:

format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: reference.docx

To make one:

  1. Start from a blank Word file, ideally one made by Quarto or Pandoc, so all the styles it uses are already there.
  2. Change the styles you care about. Don’t add any body text.
  3. Save it as reference.docx in your project or a shared template folder.

To stop colleagues using formatting the template doesn’t support, you can limit them to its styles with Review → Restrict Editing.

Callouts and other Quarto features

You can type Quarto syntax straight into Word and it will work once the document is converted. For example, this text in a Word document becomes a warning callout:

::: {.callout-warning}
# Warning!
This is a callout warning.
:::

It isn’t pretty to read in Word, so use it sparingly.

Hiding placeholders and markers

Placeholders and draft markers are easier to live with if Word can hide them. Give them a character style with the Hidden font setting, and they disappear until someone clicks ¶ on the Home tab (or presses Ctrl + Shift + 8).

To create the style: Home → Styles → New Style, set the style type to Character, then Format → Font and tick Hidden.

The package includes a Word document that already has these styles:

system.file("extdata", "PlaceholderMarker_example.docx", package = "knittogether")

Think about whether hiding helps the people editing the document. Text you can’t see is easy to delete by accident, and a deleted marker means that output can’t be refreshed. For HTML output, hide_markers_css() hides the markers in the same way.
